reference.source: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
clinicalPearls: Medial knee pain and tenderness below the joint line at the insertion of the pes anserinus (sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus)
Common in middle-aged and older people, those with knee osteoarthritis or obesity, and in some athletes, especially with valgus loading
Pain is typically inferomedial to the joint line, helping distinguish it from medial joint-line pathology
Frequently overlaps with or is secondary to medial compartment osteoarthritis
Ultrasound may show bursal fluid, though the diagnosis is largely clinical and imaging often serves to exclude other causes
Management is conservative with load and activity modification and addressing biomechanics and the hamstrings and adductors with physiotherapy; corticosteroid injection may help resistant cases
Consider referred pain and intra-articular pathology when the picture is atypical
reference.pathophysiology: The pes anserine bursa lies deep to the conjoined insertion of sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus on the anteromedial proximal tibia. Friction and overload from repetitive knee flexion and extension, valgus stress, tight hamstrings and altered biomechanics irritate the bursa. It is commonly associated with medial compartment osteoarthritis and with obesity and can be difficult to separate from these, forming part of a medial knee overload picture rather than always an isolated inflammatory bursitis.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical localisation of tenderness inferomedial to the joint line
Ultrasound to assess for bursal fluid and adjacent structures
MRI where meniscal, ligamentous or bony pathology is suspected
Weight-bearing radiographs to assess medial compartment osteoarthritis
Assessment of lower-limb biomechanics and alignment
redFlags: Features suggesting a fracture such as focal bone tenderness in an at-risk athlete
Locking or true mechanical symptoms suggesting meniscal pathology
Systemic features suggesting infection or inflammatory arthritis
A marked joint effusion suggesting intra-articular pathology
reference.prognosis: Generally responds to conservative management and correction of contributing factors, although it may persist or recur when associated osteoarthritis or biomechanical factors remain.
pitfalls: Attributing all medial knee pain to the bursa while missing osteoarthritis or meniscal disease
Over-reliance on imaging when the diagnosis is clinical
Neglecting biomechanical contributors and weight management
Repeated injection without addressing the underlying cause
references: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
